1.pericope_label: Israel relapses and Jabin oppresses them

schools.summary: Gill traces the relapse to the long rest itself, as often happens with a people favoured with plenty, who abuse their mercies and forget the giver; the principal evil, though the text does not name it, was idolatry.

Henry draws three observations from the relapse — the strange strength of corruption, which hurries men into sin despite the most frequent experience of its fatal consequences; the common ill effects of a long peace, eighty years of rest having made Israel secure and wanton where they should have been confirmed in religion; and the loss a people sustains when good governors die, the verse being readable as saying that they did evil because Ehud was dead, having feared him more than they feared God. He also counts three things that made this servitude worse than any before it: the enemy was nearer, within their borders and their bowels; he was a native of the country with an implacable enmity for the invasion that had dispossessed him; and these Canaanites had been conquered once already and might have been under Israel's feet still, so that to be oppressed by those their fathers had subdued and they themselves had foolishly spared could not but be very grievous. Behind it all he sets a single principle: they alienated themselves from God as if he were none of theirs, and God alienated them as none of his, for those who throw themselves out of his service throw themselves out of his protection.

Clarke asks why the relapse is dated from Ehud's death and not from Shamgar's, and takes the silence to intimate that Shamgar was never reckoned in the number of the judges. He supposes this Jabin a descendant of the king Joshua defeated, who had gathered the wrecks of that army, and explains the nine hundred chariots as shod with iron rather than made of it throughout, or fitted with scythes projecting from the axle by which infantry could be cut down.

Ellicott takes Jabin for a dynastic name, meaning he is wise, borne as Pharaoh and Abimelech and Agag were borne, and states at length the difficulty this chapter raises against Joshua 11: in both accounts a Jabin king of Hazor, in both subordinate kings, in both chariots prominent, and even some of the same names among the conquered. He offers two ways out and presses neither — either Hazor rose again from its ashes in the century and a half since Joshua's death under a new settlement whose king took the old dynastic name, or, if the period of the Judges must be shortened, the armies of Joshua and Barak attacked from different directions in one campaign, each tribal record preserving only the part its own people fought in. He closes on the principle that we must remember the antiquity and the fragmentary nature of these records, which were written with other and far higher views than furnishing us an elaborate consecutive history. Keil holds that the song of the next chapter is a commentary on the event rather than the quarry the prose was dug from, since the prose carries details for which we look in the song in vain.

debates.question: Why is the relapse dated from the death of Ehud?

positions.position: because a good governor restrains a people who fear him more than they fear God, so that they revolted as soon as his strict eye was gone
the harder question is why Ehud and not Shamgar, which intimates that Shamgar was never counted among the judges

debates.question: How is this Jabin related to the Jabin Joshua defeated?

positions.position: a descendant of that king, who had gathered the wrecks of the old army
Jabin is a dynastic title, and either Hazor was rebuilt under a new settlement or the two campaigns are one event preserved in two tribal records

outliers.note: holds that the prose account is not derived from Deborah's song, since it preserves details the song lacks

themes: why the relapse followed the rest
whether this Jabin is the Jabin of Joshua 11
the nine hundred chariots of iron

4.pericope_label: Deborah the prophetess judging under her palm

schools.summary: Gill takes Deborah's name to mean bee, and Lapidoth to be her husband's name, dismissing the Jewish notion that the husband was Barak himself on the strength of a likeness in the names, Barak meaning lightning and Lapidoth lamps. Of the tree he allows that her dwelling house may have stood under a palm, but thinks it likelier she sat under one in the open air when the people came to her with their cases, and that it took her name from that; he records from Abarbanel the alternative that it was called after Rebekah's nurse Deborah, who was buried near Bethel.

Henry says she answered her name in her industry and sagacity and her great usefulness to the public, her sweetness to her friends and her sharpness to her enemies. He defines her office narrowly: she judged not as a princess, by civil authority conferred upon her, but as a prophetess and as God's mouth to the people, correcting abuses and redressing grievances, especially such as concerned the worship of God, so that men came to her less for the deciding of controversies between neighbours than for advice about what was amiss in things pertaining to God. He allows either that she had her house beneath the palm, a mean habitation that would couch under a tree, or that she had her judgment-seat in the open air under its shadow — an emblem of the justice she administered there, which thrives and grows against opposition as palms do under pressure. He passes on Rashi's alternative that she was called a woman of lamps from making the wicks for the sanctuary, and adds that having stooped to that mean office for God she was afterwards thus preferred; and he guesses that being a woman she was the more easily permitted by the oppressor to judge at all.

Clarke says the original may as well be rendered a woman of Lapidoth as the wife of Lapidoth, and calls this the first instance of female government on record, Deborah appearing supreme in civil and religious affairs alike while Lapidoth appears to have had no hand in the government. Of the tree he notes only that it is common for the Hindoos to plant trees in the names of themselves and their friends, and that some religious mendicants live for a considerable time under trees.

Ellicott quotes Cornelius à Lapide for the sense of the name, that she had a sting for foes and honey for friends, and prefers the wife of Lapidoth, the phrase closely resembling Huldah the prophetess, wife of Shallum. He marks how singular she is: the only female judge, indeed the only female ruler of any kind in Jewish history apart from Athaliah, and the only judge to whom the title prophet is expressly given, a title implying poetic as well as prophetic gifts and justified in her by her predictions, her lofty courage and the splendour of her song. Looking abroad for parallels — the Teutonic prophetesses Veleda and Alaurinia, and Joan of Arc — he marks the difference, that among the Jews prophetesses were the exception and among the ancient Germans the rule. He observes that the Hebrew says she was sitting rather than dwelling, which may mean only that she took her station under that solitary and well-known tree when giving judgment, as Abraham lived under the oak of Mamre and Saul under the pomegranate of Migron; he draws out Dean Stanley's contrast between the triumphant mother of Israel under her palm and Judaea Capta on the coins of Titus, a weeping woman seated under a palm tree with downcast eyes and folded hands and extinguished hopes; and he notes that unlike Veleda, who lived in a tower in awful seclusion, Deborah allowed the freest access to her presence. Keil reads her seat under the palm as the securing of her people's rights at home, and the summons of Barak as the securing of them against their foes abroad.

debates.question: Is Lapidoth a husband, a place, or a description?

positions.position: her husband's name, which the parallel of Huldah the prophetess, wife of Shallum, supports
the original may as well be rendered a woman of Lapidoth, that is of the place
on Rashi's reading, a woman of lamps, so called from making the wicks for the lamps of the sanctuary

a woman judging Israel
the palm tree as a seat of judgment

6.pericope_label: Barak summoned to Tabor, and the prize withdrawn

schools.summary: Gill notes that in sending for Barak, Deborah acted not as a private person but as a judge in Israel exercising public power and authority, and that the summons itself tells against the notion that Barak was her husband, since a wife and husband would have lived together. On the promise to draw Sisera to the Kishon he observes that it is the Lord speaking by Deborah, and that the drawing would be done by the secret and powerful influence of his providence, so ordering things and working on the mind of the Canaanite general as to engage him to come. Of Deborah's answer he says she made no hesitation, perceiving some degree of weakness in Barak and yet a hearty and sincere inclination to engage in the work, and would not let her absence hinder it.

Clarke reads the appointment as further evidence of Deborah's standing, since to name the general of the armies is the act of one who possesses the supreme power in the state. On Tabor he quotes Maundrell at length — a mountain standing by itself two or three furlongs within the plain of Esdraelon, with a fertile oval area at the top one furlong broad and two long, a prospect reaching to the Mediterranean, and an ascent so difficult that it took an hour to climb, which with the grand area at the summit made a very proper place for the rendezvous of Barak's army — and adds Maundrell's conjecture that the stars fighting against Sisera means the rains that swelled the Kishon at the mountain's foot until it swept his host away. On the sentence he takes the woman to be Jael rather than Deborah, and defends Barak: the Greek addition shows only that he was certain of his call but not of its timing, and wished the woman on whom the Divine Spirit constantly rested to tell him when to strike the blow he knew would be decisive, which is quite natural and quite reasonable and no impeachment whatever of his faith.

Ellicott finds Barak's quality in the summons itself, since Kedesh lay in the far north and the fact that his fame had reached the southern limits of Ephraim shows he must have been a man of great mark; his name means lightning, as does Barca, the family name of Hannibal and Hasdrubal, and Virgil calls the Scipios two lightnings of war. On the word rendered draw he is candid that the meaning is uncertain, the versions dividing between depart, lead and spread out, and takes it probably to mean that Barak was to gather his troops in small contingents so as to prevent suspicion. Tabor he describes as a strong and easily fortified hill whose broad flat top would serve the double purpose of a watch-post and a stronghold, a truncated cone of limestone rising isolated from the plain nearly nineteen hundred feet. Of the Kishon he notes that the word is nachal, not a river but a torrent-bed, the Arabic wady, and that it is always named in connection with this victory because the overthrow of Canaan was due in great measure to the providential swelling of the torrent-waters, which turned its banks into a morass and rendered the iron chariots worse than useless; it is now called the Mukatta, the river of slaughter. He calls the Greek addition to Barak's answer a sort of excuse for his want of perfect faith, renders the sentence upon him as meaning that his pre-eminence shall not be on the path which he enters, and reminds us of the humble and almost down-trodden position of women in the East, so that a great warrior could hardly fail to feel the humiliation. Keil denies that Barak's condition sprang from distrust of the divine promise: his mistrust was of his own strength, and what he wanted was the divine enthusiasm which the prophetess's presence would infuse into him and into the army gathered round him.

a want of perfect faith, for which the Greek addition to his answer is a sort of excuse
no impeachment whatever of his faith; he knew his call but not the day, and wanted her to name it

outliers.note: reads the obscure verb rendered draw as a military order, that Barak was to gather his contingents a few at a time so as not to rouse suspicion

10.pericope_label: The ten thousand mustered, and Heber's tent by Kedesh

schools.summary: Gill supposes the muster was raised either by the sound of a trumpet, as Ehud raised his, or by messengers sent to the two tribes to collect ten thousand men, who accordingly came to him at Kedesh. Of Heber he says only that he was a descendant of Kain and a principal man among the Midianites, whom the Targum calls the Salmaean.

Henry gets his good out of the phrase at his feet either way it is taken: God is said to call us to his feet, that is, into obedience to him, and the men at Barak's feet were cheerful and ready to follow him whithersoever he went. If it means they were all footmen, as he thinks it may, the disproportion of strength against horses and chariots was thereby made very great and the victory the more illustrious, the presence of God and his prophetess being abundantly sufficient to balance it. Reading the song of the next chapter back into the muster, he finds that some came in from Manasseh and Issachar, and that more were expected from Reuben, Dan and Asher who never came; the narrative here overlooks them all and tells us only that to make the ten thousand effective indeed Deborah went up with him. He explains why Heber is introduced in the middle of a muster: the removal of this one Kenite family out of the wilderness of Judah in the south into the northern country is set down for the sake of what is to follow about Jael.
Clarke says flatly that the ten thousand were footmen, since Barak had no chariots and his army was composed wholly of infantry.

Ellicott observes that the verb used is the technical word for summoning an army, and that in the first instance it will have been only the leaders of those tribes who were invited to a conference, like those of the Swiss on the Rütli in 1307; he will not have the idiom at his feet carry more than after him, as the same book renders it a few verses later. He notices which tribes answered and why: Zebulun and Naphtali would be harder to arouse than the central tribes, for though they felt the oppression most they would also have to bear the brunt of the vengeance in case of defeat, whereas Ephraim and Benjamin, stronger and more secure, could raise their contingents without the personal help of Deborah; and he suggests that a trace of her going up may survive in the name Debarieh, a village at the foot of Tabor. On the Kenite verse he corrects the version twice over — the Hebrew says not that Heber was of the children of Hobab but that he had separated himself from them, nomadic settlements being constantly liable to send off such colonies, and Hobab is Moses' brother-in-law rather than his father-in-law, the words for these relationships lying close together. He also rejects the plain of Zaanaim: the word is elon, which our translators constantly render plain because they were misled by the Targums and the Vulgate, though they render the cognate allon oak, and it should be the terebinth in Zaanaim — a tree worth naming, since the terebinths on the hills of Naphtali were fine enough to give the tribe its emblem in the blessing of Jacob. Zaanaim itself means wanderings, or the unlading of tents, which suits a nomad settlement, and he sets against it the promise that Jerusalem shall be a tent that wanders not.

positions.position: footmen — the army was all infantry, which made the victory over chariots the more illustrious
simply after him, as the same book renders the phrase a few verses later

outliers.note: corrects father in law to brother-in-law and the plain of Zaanaim to the terebinth in Zaanaim, tracing the second mistranslation to the Targums and the Vulgate

12.pericope_label: The descent from Tabor and the rout at the Kishon

schools.summary: Gill will allow either some of the Canaanites living near Tabor or spies Sisera kept out as the source of his intelligence, and mentions that some fasten it on the Kenites, who were at peace with Jabin, though whether they told him out of good will or ill will cannot be said; what is certain is that God's providence so ordered it that by one means or another he should be informed. He accounts for the gathering of the chariots by supposing they had been quartered in different places, and is careful with the word up, which cannot mean go higher, since they were already on the top of a mountain, but means bestir thyself, put the army in rank and file, and march to meet the enemy without delay. Of the rout he passes on Abarbanel's account of a noise in the heavens like the noise of a large army, with horses and chariots of fire, which he supposes terrified them before Barak came down at all, so that it plainly appeared to be the Lord's doing; and he reports from Josephus the storm of rain and hail driven into their faces, which so blinded them that their slings and arrows were useless and their armoured men too benumbed to hold a sword.

Clarke sees the whole point of Deborah's presence discharged in a single word: this is exactly what Barak wanted her for, since he did not know the day, and she told him the precise time. He renders the verb of the rout as confounded, threw them all into confusion, drove them pell-mell, so that chariots broke and overthrew chariots and universal disorder was thrown into all their ranks, leaving Barak and his men little to do but kill and pursue and forcing Sisera to abandon his chariot; and he has no doubt the whole was done by supernatural agency, God sending his angel and confounding them.

Ellicott thinks it unnecessary to guess who carried the news, since the verse about Heber was brought in by way of anticipation so that a reader who last heard of the Kenites in the south of Judah should not be surprised to meet them in Naphtali a few verses on, and the they may simply be impersonal, as the Greek and Latin have it, it was told. Sisera's gathering of all his forces he reads as the judgment of a soldier who saw at once that this very sudden revolt had assumed formidable proportions and that he would need everything he had to dislodge Barak from so strong a position. He sets the words this is the day against the practice of an age that attached the utmost importance to fortunate and unfortunate days, and marks the difference, that Barak was guided by a prophetess and not by idle auguries; and he measures what obedience cost, since with neither cavalry nor chariots it required no little faith to abandon a strong post and take the aggressive against the kind of force that struck most terror into Israelites. Of the storm he judges Josephus to be following a correct Jewish tradition, given the swollen Kishon and the tempest of the song, and he explains why the general came down from his chariot rather than fleeing in it — he had far more chance of concealment on foot than in the well-known chariot of a commander, and the vehicle was in any case probably struggling in the trampled morass. Of the pursuit he notes that a rout in which the fugitives must cross a river and fight a storm is always specially fatal, and that the memory of this carnage survived for years, together with the circumstance that the soil was enriched by the dead. Keil observes that the verb rendered discomfited is the word of Exodus and Joshua, denoting the confounding of a hostile army by a miracle of God and mostly by some miraculous phenomenon of nature, which puts Sisera's overthrow in the same category as Pharaoh's destruction.

debates.question: Who showed Sisera that Barak had gone up to Tabor?

positions.position: Canaanites living near Tabor, or Sisera's own spies, or possibly the Kenites, who were at peace with Jabin
no need to name anyone; the Kenite verse was an anticipation, and the they may be impersonal, it was told

outliers.note: sets Deborah's naming of the day against the ancient reliance on lucky and unlucky days, insisting that Barak was guided by a prophetess and not by auguries

themes: who told Sisera that Barak had gone up
this is the day
the storm that broke the chariots

schools.summary: Gill pictures Jael seeing him coming and knowing him full well, and stepping forward to invite him in; some think she had been looking out to take in any Israelite in distress, and she had very probably been some time at her tent door to inquire how the battle went, which, living so near Kedesh, she knew was expected. On the request for water he observes that thirst was natural enough after the heat of the battle and the day and the running, and considers whether Sisera avoided asking for wine because the Kenites kept none; but he answers that the abstinence of the Rechabites was enjoined later by Jonadab in the days of Jehu, so the custom had not yet obtained.

Henry follows the steps of the fall. The chariot had been Sisera's pride and his confidence, and we may suppose he had despised the armies of the living God for having neither chariot nor horse; justly then is he made ashamed of it and forced to quit it. With no strong-hold of his own in reach he flees to a way of living he had probably ridiculed, and the more because religion was kept up among the Kenites; what emboldened him was that there was no league between Jabin and Heber, only an absence of hostility, Jabin having never troubled so quiet and harmless a people — not considering that though they suffered nothing from Jabin they heartily sympathised with the Israel of God that did. Of Jael's welcome he says that in seeming to design the relieving of his fatigue she perhaps really intended the retarding of his flight, that he might fall into the hands of Barak, and it may well be questioned whether she had at first any thought of taking away his life, but rather God afterwards put it into her heart. When he desired her to say he was not there she declined making any such promise, and Henry draws the rule: we must not sin against God, no, not to oblige those we would show ourselves most observant of.

Clarke explains the choice of tent by Eastern etiquette, that no person ever intrudes into the apartments of the women, and that in every dwelling the women have a separate apartment. Of the milk he notes that she gave more than he requested, and that her friendship increased his confidence and security; and of the watch at the door, that since no man would intrude into the women's apartment, her simply saying there is no man in my tent would preclude all search.

Ellicott notes that Sisera ran in the opposite direction from his army, which made for Harosheth, and arrived a starving and ruined fugitive; women had separate tents which were regarded as inviolably secure, so that he might lie there unsuspected till the pursuers passed. Her going out to meet him he finds decisive of her intention — it makes it probable that her design was already formed, unless we suppose that Jael as a chieftainess was placed above the ordinary rules which regulate the conduct of Oriental women — and since nothing is said of Heber, he may have been absent, or may have kept out of the way in order to further his wife's designs. Without that special invitation, he adds, Sisera would not have ventured to violate every law of Oriental propriety by entering the privileged sanctuary of the harem, and her fear not was no idle word, treachery being far too common among Bedouin tribes to render the exhortation needless. He suspects the request for water, which was natural enough in itself but had not been made on arriving, and thinks Sisera wanted to taste food in the tent as a way of rendering still more secure the inviolable laws of Eastern hospitality. Soured milk he grants as likely, buttermilk being a common drink in Arab tents, but calls R. Tanchum's claim that it inebriates and Rashi's that it produces deep sleep, with the object of stupefying him, simply giving reins to the imagination. On the lie he is asked to tell, Ellicott answers that in that age and among those nations a lie would have been regarded as perfectly natural and justifiable, and that it would be very unfair to judge by the standard of Christianity the words and actions of ignorant nomads and idolatrous Canaanites more than a thousand years before Christ, when the heathen advice of Darius stood — when it is necessary to lie, lie. Keil sees in the reception nothing but the usual form of oriental hospitality: she turned him aside from the road and covered him with a rug that he might sleep, being thoroughly exhausted with his flight, and handed him milk from her skin instead of water merely for the purpose of giving her guest a friendly and hospitable reception. He dismisses as later decorations of no historical worth both Josephus's claim that the milk had already turned and R. Tanchum's that such milk intoxicated the weary man.

21.pericope_label: Jael drives the tent-peg through his temples

schools.summary: Gill accounts for the weapon by the household: there were no arms in the tent, for the Kenites used none, so she took up the iron pin by which the tent was fastened to the ground. He also supplies an inward warrant for the deed. She perceived he was fast asleep, and it was now put into her heart to kill him, an impulse upon her spirit which she was persuaded by the effect it had upon her was of God, since it filled her not with malice and revenge but with a concern for the glory of God, the interest of religion and the good of Israel.

Clarke identifies the nail as one of the spikes by which the cords of a tent are fastened to the ground, and explains why a single blow sufficed: Sisera lay on one side, overwhelmed with sleep through the heat and fatigues of the day, so that the piercing of his temples must have in a moment put him past resistance. Of Barak's arrival he will not guess further than the text does — what impression the sight made on the victor is not said, but it could not have given him much pleasure, especially when he learned the circumstances of the death.

Ellicott takes the nail for one of the great tent-pegs used to fasten down the cords, noting that Josephus calls it iron while the Greek renders it a wooden plug and nothing decides between them, and would render an hammer as the hammer, the ponderous wooden mallet kept in every tent for beating down those pegs, whose name makkebeth gave the Maccabees their title. He rejects in his strongest terms the defence that at this instant Jael received a divine intimation of what she was to do: to make such an assumption as a way of defending an act of assassination peculiarly terrible and peculiarly treacherous seems to him unwarrantable to the last degree, and those who adopt such methods for themselves ought not to press these private interpretations upon others, since a mind unsophisticated by the casuistry of exegesis will arrive at a fair estimate of her conduct without interpolating suppositions into the narrative. He wonders whether the needless words Heber's wife are emphatic, recalling the peace between Jabin and the house of Heber mentioned when the name last occurred, though he thinks it more probably due to the very ancient and inartificial character of the record. To the argument from the narrative's silence he answers that the description is exceedingly graphic and yet its silence as to any condemnation of the worst and darkest features by no means necessarily excludes the idea of the most complete disapproval, the method here being that of all ancient literature and wholly different from the modern habit of subjective reflection, as Homer sometimes relates an atrocity without a word of censure and sometimes indicates disapproval by a single casual adjective; and he takes the clause about Sisera being fast asleep and weary to be there only to account for his not being awakened by Jael's approach or her preparations, unless it involves a passing touch of pity. He ends on the tableau of the undaunted murderess standing in her tent between the dead chieftain and the living one, glorying in the decision that had flung to the winds every rule of Eastern morality and decorum. Keil grants that Deborah's word was fulfilled to the letter, the Lord having sold Sisera into the hand of a woman and deprived Barak of the glory of the victory, and still refuses the conclusion: neither that prophetic announcement nor the fact that the deed is commemorated in the song of the next chapter makes the act itself morally justified, even allowing that Jael acted under the influence of religious enthusiasm.

debates.question: Was Jael divinely directed to kill Sisera?

positions.position: yes; an impulse upon her spirit which its own effect proved to be of God, since it bred not malice but zeal for God's glory and the good of Israel
to assume a divine intimation in order to defend an assassination peculiarly terrible and treacherous is unwarrantable to the last degree
even granting religious enthusiasm, neither the prophecy nor the praise of the song makes the act morally justified

outliers.note: answers the argument from the narrative's silence by the method of ancient literature, where Homer relates an atrocity without censure and marks his judgment by a single casual adjective

whether Jael was divinely directed
the silence of the narrative

23.pericope_label: Jabin subdued, and the verdict on Jael's deed

schools.summary: Gill reports from Josephus that as Barak went towards Hazor he met Jabin, slew him and destroyed the city, the king having perhaps come out with a second army on hearing of Sisera's defeat; but he thinks what follows in the text points the other way, to a total conquest accomplished afterwards and gradually.

Clarke will not close the chapter without putting Jael's act on trial, and draws the indictment himself in ten counts: there was peace between her family and the king of Canaan, made as such treaties always were with a sacrifice and an oath; knowing this, Sisera came to her tent with the utmost confidence; she met him with the most friendly greetings and assurances of safety; she gave him more than he asked and in a vessel suited to his dignity; she hid him in the secret part of her own tent and covered him so as to evidence her good faith; she undertook to keep watch at the door and deny his presence; having sheltered and refreshed him she was bound by the rules of Asiatic hospitality to defend his life at the risk of her own; instead she took advantage of his weariness and deep sleep and took away his life, and then exulted in the deed and showed Barak in triumph what she had done. Do we not find in all this, he asks, bad faith, deceit, deep hypocrisy, lying, breach of treaty, contempt of religious rites, breach of the laws of hospitality, deliberate and unprovoked murder? The one defence ever offered is that she was sincere at first and afterwards divinely directed, which would vindicate her by the fact, since God has a right to dispose of the lives of his creatures as he pleases and the cup of Sisera's iniquity was probably full; but there is no sufficient evidence that she received any such direction, Jael says nothing of her motives, and the sacred penman says nothing either, but states the fact as he stated Ehud's and leaves his readers to form their own opinion. He rejects the plea that a public enemy may be killed by any of the people he oppresses as a very dangerous position, which refers one of the most solemn acts of judgment and justice to the caprice or prejudice of every individual who may persuade himself that he is authorised by God to take vengeance by his own hand; and his own verdict is a refusal of verdict — I will not justify, I dare not absolutely condemn; there I leave them. On the closing verse he construes the Hebrew as it went, going, and takes it to mean that Israel followed up the victory until the kingdom as well as the king was destroyed.

Ellicott notes that the name used here is Elohim while Jehovah occurs through the rest of the narrative, and says plainly that we are not yet in a position to formulate the law which regulates the interchange of these names. He then denies that the verse settles anything about Jael: this attribution of the deliverance to God's providence and aid does not necessarily involve the least approval of the false and cruel elements which stained her courage and faith, for though God overrules even criminal acts to the fulfilment of his own purposes, the crimes themselves meet with their own just condemnation and retribution. The case of Jehu he calls decisive — conduct likewise of a mixed character, an instrument in the hands of God to punish and overthrow the guilty house of Ahab, showing dauntlessness and faith in carrying out that commission, and yet justly condemned by the voice of the prophet for his atrocious cruelty, as Baasha had been before him. To explain this clause and the triumphal cry of Deborah, so let all thine enemies perish, as Bishop Wordsworth does, to mean that the work of Jael is represented by the sacred writer as the work of God, is to claim divine sanction for a wish that wicked or hostile powers should always so perish by cruel and treacherous assassination. At the same time he refuses the opposite excess: Jael must not be classed with women actuated only by a demoniacal thirst for vengeance, like Criemhild in the Nibelungenlied, nor even with Aretophila of Cyrene whom Plutarch so emphatically praises, but rather with women like Judith in ancient and Charlotte Corday in modern times, who regarded themselves as the champions of a great and good cause. Of the closing verse he gives the same literal rendering, the hand going went and was hard, that is became heavier and heavier in its pressure, and calls the battle of the Kishon the beginning of a complete deliverance of Israel from the yoke of the Canaanites. Keil reads the same idiom as denoting the continual increase of the pressure until they had destroyed him, and warns that the overthrow of Jabin and his rule did not involve the extermination of the Canaanites generally.

debates.question: Was Jabin destroyed at once or gradually?

positions.position: at once, Barak meeting and slaying him on the way to Hazor and destroying the city, as Josephus reports
gradually, the hand of Israel pressing heavier and heavier until they had destroyed him

debates.question: How is Jael's deed finally to be judged?

positions.position: the facts amount to bad faith, breach of treaty and hospitality, and deliberate murder; without evidence of a divine direction he will not justify her, and dares not absolutely condemn

the crime meets its own condemnation though God overruled it, as with Jehu; yet she belongs with those who took themselves for champions of a good cause, not with women moved by a thirst for vengeance

outliers.note: notices that the deliverance is credited here to Elohim where the rest of the narrative says Jehovah, and declines to formulate any law for the interchange
